title: Queen Elizabeth’s Final Diary Entry Before Her Death Was Surprisingly Simple
subtitle: In just a few short words, she summed up her entire duty to the Crown
author: Katie Robinson

annotations.comment: This article felt machine-generated because of how many different adjectives they used for "says". The conclusion also contained the very common AI phrase "In a world".
There are few clues here. I have based my choice on a few phrases that "sound human", namely, "held fast to the quiet routines" and "In a world now accustomed to oversharing."
It's well-written and there aren't any grammatical issues with it, but it isn't as stiff as AI. It has personality. It also uses contractions and a filler words, although sparse.

I am confident this is AI-generated. The lead in doesn't provide context for who Queen Elizabeth II is, and the lead in already gets to the point, leaving the rest of the article to be fluff-filled sentiments. If I am correct, it also gets the topic of the article wrong; it shouldn't be about some grand statement about oversharing, but the article should have been about Elizabeth herself and who she is... Also, the sentence about "gave [her] a chance to keep track of [events, meetings, and impressions] without imposing interpretation or sentiment." really describes AI's language in a nutshell. No matter how much editing is done, anything it writes that's related to present information on a topic, it's always imposing its interpretation and sentiment through its language and writing structure (and whether that's based on company policies integrated into the model, its own algorithm, or a mixture of the two, I am not certain, but it's just my opinion either way)

Laborious structure of sentence 1 in the final paragraph. 
Competently written but AI should be trained to refrain from mawkish elaboration.
